newsitem.title: CUBA: Peru's Fujimori makes surprise trip to Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori makes surprise trip to Cuba.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori arrived in Cuba on Monday on a surprise trip that is expected to include discussions of Peru's hostage crisis with President Fidel Castro.
Fujimori, who flew in from the Dominican Republic, was met at Havana's Jose Marti airport by Castro and other senior government officials.

The Peruvian leader was believed to be hoping to discuss ways of resolving the 76-day-old hostage crisis, in which some 20 Marxist rebels are holding 72 men hostage at the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima. Fujimori had flown to Santo Domingo on Sunday afternoon on a quick trip to talk about the crisis in Lima.
Fujimori's arrival in Havana capped weeks of speculation that Cuba might be asked to play a role to end Latin America's longest hostage crisis.

But Cuba has declined all comment on such speculation. Cuban government officials on Monday made no immediate comment on the purpose of Fujimori's visit and did not even confirm the Peruvian leader was coming until his plane arrived.
Foreign Ministry officials told foreign reporters Fujimori would go straight to the Council of State, where Castro traditionally receives visitors.
The officials said a news conference was scheduled at the Council of State for the early afternoon. However, they gave no other details.
Fujimori had been thought to be returning directly to Lima on Monday after visiting the Dominican Republic, where he held a 3-1/2 hour meeting on Sunday with President Leonel Fernandez.

Peru-based journalists who travelled on a separate plane to cover Fujimori's trip to the Dominican Republic arrived in Havana just before the Peruvian leader. They said they were completely unaware of where they were going until shortly before arriving in Cuba.
News reports have said Cuba, Nicaragua or a country in Eastern Europe could be potential places of asylum for the rebels.

While ruling out considering the main demand of the rebels -- the release of 400 jailed comrades -- Fujimori has indicated he might make other concessions. He has always left the way open to asylum in another country for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary (MRTA) rebels, who seized their captives on Dec 17.

From the start, Cuba was cited in foreign news reports as a possible mediator in the crisis, or as a place of refuge for the rebels. The MRTA is said to be inspired by Cuba's revolution but it is not known to have any links with Havana.

Castro mediated in June 1995 to secure the freedom of the brother of former Colombian president Cesar Gaviria, kidnapped by a Colombian guerrilla group. Some of the kidnappers and their families flew to Cuba.
Havana also intervened to help resolve a crisis in Colombia in 1980 when guerrillas of the M-19 movement seized 14 ambassadors at the Dominican embassy residence in Bogota.
That siege lasted two months and ended without bloodshed when the guerrillas dropped their demands and freed their hostages, flying to Cuba in a plane sent by Castro.
The heavily armed squad of mainly teenage MRTA rebels originally took hundreds of hostages when they stormed a cocktail party at the Japanese ambassador's residence.
They freed most captives in the first few weeks of the crisis. Two Cuban diplomats were among the original hostages freed in that initial period.
But the hostage takers still hold two of Fujimori's relatives, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
